head.title: SQL Island Sequel - Collector's Archive (T7)
head.teaser: SQL Island and the Collector's Archive: Bringing order into chaotic data (SQL Window Functions)
head.copyright: Rino Moreno Albertin, Lana Cvijic, Joël Tauss, Endrit Nazifi © CC BY 4.0

text-scene.text: Life on SQL Island had become almost predictable. SQLaus knew the roads between the villages, the villagers knew his face, and the island’s tables had become familiar enough to feel trustworthy.

That routine changed one morning when several sealed crates and wrapped bundles of documents were discovered at the shore near Onionville. No ship had been seen during the night, and no villager claimed to know where the delivery had come from. Yet the contents were unmistakably deliberate: copied ledgers, valuation lists, and carefully structured catalogue fragments connected to a collector of rare objects.

“These are not ordinary island records,” SQLaus said after reading the first few pages. A short note accompanied the archive material: “A true collection is not merely counted. It is ordered.” The signature identified the sender simply as the Collector.

The message was short but the material itself revealed a very clear intention. Certain inhabitants had been marked as unusually interesting, some villages appeared repeatedly in the records, while others were mentioned only in passing.
As SQLaus read further, he realized that the archive was not designed to produce simple totals, but to preserve order, rarity, and relative position. Some entries had to be ranked within categories, others compared to earlier or later acquisitions, and several only became meaningful when viewed in the context of the records around them. A summarized result would have hidden exactly the structure that made the archive valuable.
He folded the note and looked back at the catalogue pages. “To analyze this archive, I will need window functions.”

select-scene.text:
Mission 0: Opening the Collector's Archive
Before SQLaus can bring order to the Collector's records, he first needs to inspect the archive itself. Display the complete collector_archive table so he can study the available entries, categories, values, and recorded dates.

Mission 1: Cataloguing the Inhabitants
After reading the Collector’s note, SQLaus realizes that the archive is not meant to simply list information, but to impose a clear and consistent structure.
“To understand the archive,” he says. “I must first bring order to the inhabitants themselves.”
The Collector first wants a stable archive order. SQLaus must assign a sequential catalogue number to every inhabitant within each village, ordered alphabetically by name.
This ensures that each village has its own internal structure and that no ambiguity remains in how inhabitants are organized.
The result should include: - village_name - inhabitant_name - catalogue_number
Tables: inhabitant, village
Functions: ROW_NUMBER() with PARTITION BY, ORDER BY
select-scene.sql-solution: SELECT v.name AS village_name, i.name AS inhabitant_name, ROW_NUMBER() OVER ( PARTITION BY i.villageid ORDER BY i.name ) AS catalogue_number FROM inhabitant i INNER JOIN village v ON i.villageid = v.id;
select-scene.sql-placeholder: SELECT v.name AS village_name, i.name AS inhabitant_name, ... OVER ( PARTITION BY ... ORDER BY ... ) AS catalogue_number FROM inhabitant i INNER JOIN village v ON i.villageid = v.id;

select-scene.text:
Mission 2: Ranking the Most Valuable Curiosities
With the inhabitants now properly ordered within their villages, SQLaus turns his attention to the broader structure of the archive.
“Order alone is not enough,” he notes. “The Collector clearly values comparison.”
The Collector wants a global prestige ranking of all inhabitants by gold. If two inhabitants have the same amount, they should share the same place, with gaps in the following rank positions.
This ranking reveals the relative importance of inhabitants across the entire archive, highlighting those of highest value.
The result should include: - inhabitant_name - village_name - gold - prestige_rank
Tables: inhabitant, village
Functions: RANK() with ORDER BY
select-scene.sql-solution: SELECT i.name AS inhabitant_name, v.name AS village_name, i.gold, RANK() OVER ( ORDER BY i.gold DESC ) AS prestige_rank FROM inhabitant i INNER JOIN village v ON i.villageid = v.id;
select-scene.sql-placeholder: SELECT i.name AS inhabitant_name, v.name AS village_name, i.gold, ... AS prestige_rank FROM inhabitant i INNER JOIN village v ON i.villageid = v.id;

select-scene.text:
Mission 3: Compact Village Display
As SQLaus prepares a public display of the Collector’s notes, he notices a small but awkward problem. Whenever two inhabitants from the same village own the same amount of gold, the ranking leaves gaps and makes the exhibition look untidy.
“That will not do,” he says. “Equal wealth may share a place, but the list itself should remain compact.”
The Collector therefore asks for a village-wise ranking of inhabitants by gold, using consecutive rank numbers even when ties occur.
The result should include: - inhabitant_name - village_name - gold - village_rank
Method hint: Work within each village, order inhabitants by gold descending, and use DENSE_RANK() to create a compact ranking without gaps.
select-scene.sql-solution: SELECT i.name AS inhabitant_name, v.name AS village_name, i.gold, DENSE_RANK() OVER ( PARTITION BY i.villageid ORDER BY i.gold DESC ) AS village_rank FROM inhabitant i INNER JOIN village v ON i.villageid = v.id;
select-scene.sql-placeholder: SELECT i.name AS inhabitant_name, v.name AS village_name, i.gold, ... AS village_rank FROM inhabitant i INNER JOIN village v ON i.villageid = v.id;

text-scene.text:
The village display falls neatly into place.
SQLaus studies the compact ranks and nods. What had looked awkward before now reads like a proper exhibition list.
“Good,” he says. “Now the pattern is clear at a glance.”

select-scene.text:
Mission 4: Tracing Village Contribution Values
The longer SQLaus studies the Archive, the clearer it becomes that the Collector cared not only about isolated objects, but also about how each village contributed to the archive over time.
To inspect this contribution history, SQLaus wants to follow the archive entries village by village. For every contribution, he compares its estimated value with the estimated value of the previous contribution from the same village.
This helps him see how the value of each village's contributions changed from one recorded entry to the next.
For this, the output should contain: - village_name - recorded_day - description - estimated_value - value_change_from_previous
Method hint: Join the archive with the villages, work within each village, order the entries by recorded day and entryid, and use LAG() to compare the current estimated value with the previous one.
select-scene.sql-solution: SELECT v.name AS village_name, ca.recorded_day, ca.description, ca.estimated_value, ca.estimated_value - LAG(ca.estimated_value) OVER ( PARTITION BY ca.villageid ORDER BY ca.recorded_day, ca.id ) AS value_change_from_previous FROM collector_archive ca INNER JOIN village v ON ca.villageid = v.id ORDER BY ca.villageid, ca.recorded_day, ca.id;
select-scene.sql-placeholder: SELECT v.name AS village_name, ca.recorded_day, ca.description, ca.estimated_value, ... AS value_change_from_previous FROM collector_archive ca INNER JOIN village v ON ca.villageid = v.id ORDER BY ca.villageid, ca.recorded_day, ca.id;

text-scene.text:
The village contribution history becomes visible.
SQLaus follows the archive entries village by village and compares each contribution with the previous one from the same village. Some values rise sharply, while others fall again.

manipulate-scene.text:
Mission 5: Updating the records with the next Acquisition.
The Collector wants to see which entry comes next in each category, according to the record date. Because there is an empty column in the records for a key pointing to the next item, SQLaus wants to add said information into the concerning column named next_entryid. This should make the archive more comprehensible.
Method hint: Use a CTE or Subquery to wrap the window function to be able to use it in an update clause.
manipulate-scene.sql-solution: WITH next_entries AS ( SELECT id, LEAD(id) OVER (PARTITION BY category ORDER BY recorded_day) AS next_entryid FROM collector_archive ) UPDATE collector_archive ca SET next_entryid = ne.next_entryid FROM next_entries ne WHERE ca.id = ne.id;
manipulate-scene.sql-check:
WITH next_entries AS ( SELECT id, LEAD(id) OVER (PARTITION BY category ORDER BY recorded_day) AS next_entryid FROM collector_archive )
SELECT ca.id, ca.next_entryid FROM collector_archive ca INNER JOIN next_entries ne on ca.id = ne.id where ca.next_entryid = ne.next_entryid;
manipulate-scene.sql-placeholder: WITH next_entries AS ( SELECT id, ... AS next_entryid FROM collector_archive ) UPDATE collector_archive ca SET ... FROM next_entries ne WHERE ...

text-scene.text: SQLaus writes down the next entries in the records in the notebook. Now, that this information is logged for each item, it makes it easier to follow when and in which order items were added.

select-scene.text:
Mission 6: Item recency in categories
After browsing through the archive documents and records for a while, SQLaus wonders: "When were the different entries added to the categories? I wonder how far they spread out over time." In order to find that out, he wants to see the first and last entry per category (according to the recorded_day), one row per category to keep things tidy.
Giving it some thought, SQLaus decides that the following columns should be displayed: - category - first_recorded_day - last_recorded_day
Method hint: First, write the query for the first and last value to see if it works, then wrap it again in a CTE or a subquery to use the values to join the other tables.
select-scene.sql-solution:
WITH cat_first_last AS (
SELECT DISTINCT category,
FIRST_VALUE(id) OVER ( PARTITION BY category ORDER BY recorded_day ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING ) AS first_entryid,
LAST_VALUE(id) OVER ( PARTITION BY category ORDER BY recorded_day ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING ) AS last_entryid
FROM collector_archive ) SELECT cfl.category, ca_first.recorded_day AS first_recorded_day, ca_last.recorded_day AS last_recorded_day FROM cat_first_last AS cfl INNER JOIN collector_archive AS ca_first on cfl.first_entryid = ca_first.id INNER JOIN collector_archive AS ca_last on cfl.last_entryid = ca_last.id ;
select-scene.sql-placeholder:
WITH cat_first_last AS (
SELECT DISTINCT category,
... AS first_entryid,
... AS last_entryid
FROM collector_archive ) SELECT cfl.category, ca_first.recorded_day AS first_recorded_day, ca_last.recorded_day AS last_recorded_day FROM cat_first_last AS cfl INNER JOIN collector_archive AS ca_first on ... INNER JOIN collector_archive AS ca_last on ... ;

text-scene.text: No big differences emerge. It seems that for all categories the oldest and most recent items were added around the same time, implying there is no category which has been less active or of less recent interest to the Collector. Nevertheless, it is interesting to see.

select-scene.text:
Mission 7: The Third-Rarest Standard
While studying the Archive, SQLaus noticed that the Collector does not compare items randomly. Instead, he uses a fixed benchmark: the third entry in descending rarity within each category.
“This is the standard,” SQLaus murmurs. “Not the rarest… but the point of balance.” To understand the Collector's logic, SQLaus must display every archive entry together with this benchmark value for its category.
To do so, he needs to display the following columns: - category - description - rarity_score - third_highest_rarity (the third value in descending rarity order within the category)
Method hint: Use a window function to work within each category by partitioning the data with PARTITION BY and ordering entries by rarity_score in descending order. Then apply a function like NTH_VALUE() to retrieve the third value in this order. Make sure the window frame includes all rows in the partition so the result is the same for every row. Remember, you are not filtering rows but adding the third highest rarity as a constant reference for each category.
select-scene.sql-solution: SELECT category, description, rarity_score, NTH_VALUE(rarity_score, 3) OVER ( PARTITION BY category ORDER BY rarity_score DESC, id ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING ) AS third_highest_rarity FROM collector_archive;
select-scene.sql-placeholder: SELECT category, description, rarity_score, ... AS third_highest_rarity FROM collector_archive;

text-scene.text:
The hidden benchmark appears at last.
SQLaus realizes that the Collector never focused only on extremes, but instead compared every item against a stable internal standard.
“You're starting to understand,” he murmurs.

select-scene.text:
Mission 8: The Collector's Prestige Tiers
The Collector now wants the archive to be easier to understand at a glance.
A long list of values is useful for experts, but visitors need structure. Each category must therefore be divided into three prestige tiers based on estimated value.
SQLaus must split the entries of every category into three groups, ordering them from highest to lowest value, so that each item receives a tier relative to others in the same category.
To do so, he needs to display the following columns: - category - description - estimated_value - prestige_tier
Method hint: Work within each category, order by estimated value descending and divide the rows into three groups.
select-scene.sql-solution: SELECT category, description, estimated_value, NTILE(3) OVER ( PARTITION BY category ORDER BY estimated_value DESC, id ) AS prestige_tier FROM collector_archive;
select-scene.sql-placeholder: SELECT category, description, estimated_value, ... AS prestige_tier FROM collector_archive;

text-scene.text:
The archive now reveals its final form.
What once seemed like scattered records has become a clear structure of tiers, standards, and relationships.
SQLaus leans back and smiles. “You did it. You didn't just read the archive — you understood it!”
Congratulations! You solved all missions and helped SQLaus bring order to the Collector's archive.

You have successfully applied window functions to uncover patterns within the data. Here is a short summary of the techniques you used during this game: - assigning ordered positions within groups - ranking and comparing values - analyzing changes over time - retrieving specific reference points within partitions - dividing data into meaningful tiers
Through this game, you did not simply query the archive — you understood how to work with the data in context.
